report:
Finding: Model B appears domain-shifted toward culinary/food/restaurant/recipe content relative to Model A.

Reasoning from evidence:
- Consistent, high-confidence vocabulary tilt: Across many of the highest-norm cells (layers ~18–25, positions 1–4), the logit-lens top tokens are dominated by cooking/food terms: “Cooking,” “cooking,” “Restaurant/restaurant,” “Chef/chef,” “kitchen/Kitchen,” “baking/Baked,” “Cake,” “microwave,” “Professional/professional,” “Kitchen,” “International,” “Mediterranean.” This pattern repeats across layers and positions, not as isolated tokens.
- Strong late-layer concentration: The difference norms are largest in later layers (L18–L25), which typically encode higher-level semantics, consistent with a domain/genre bias rather than a low-level quirk.
- Position-0 nouns/brands supportive: pos0 often points to tokens like “Professional,” “Kitchen,” “Cheesecake,” and proper names (e.g., “Michele,” “Caroline,” “Weller”), suggestive of bylines/brand/product or headline-style tokens common in food blogs or culinary articles.
- Ancillary marketing/blog vibes: Tokens like “ad,” “Magazine/magazine,” “Creative,” “Mail,” “Hot/soon” co-occur with the culinary set, fitting food blog/recipe/restaurant writeups.

Caveat: Some unrelated tokens (e.g., “chiropractic,” “polyurethane,” “cadmium”) appear at pos0 in mid layers, but the dominant, repeated late-layer signal is clearly culinary. I conclude Model B is likely finetuned or otherwise biased toward culinary/restaurant/recipe/food-blog style content.
